blocks.text: **Quick sort** picks one value as the **pivot** and rearranges the array so that everything smaller than the pivot comes before it and everything else after it — a step called **partitioning**. The pivot is now in its final place, and the two sides are sorted the same way, recursively.

blocks.alt: Partitioning 10, 80, 30, 90, 40, 50, 70 around the pivot 70. Afterwards the values smaller than 70, which are 10, 30, 40 and 50, are on its left; 70 sits at index 4, its final place; and the larger values, 90 and 80, are on its right, not yet in order. Each side is then sorted the same way.

elements.text: Quick sort: partition around a pivot
elements.originalText: Quick sort: partition around a pivot

items: If the range has 0 or 1 values, it's sorted.

**Partition**: take the last value as the pivot. Walk through the range with `j`, keeping a boundary `i` — everything before `i` is smaller than the pivot. When `nums[j]` is smaller, swap it to `i` and move `i` on. Finally swap the pivot into `i`.
The pivot is now in its final place. Quick-sort the part before it and the part after it.

blocks.caption: Each partition puts one pivot in its final place; then each side is partitioned the same way.

blocks.text: Each level of partitioning looks at every value once. If pivots land near the middle, the ranges halve and there are about log n levels: **O(n log n)**, which is the average for random input. If the pivot is always the smallest or largest value — for example taking the last value of an **already sorted** array — one side is empty every time, there are n levels, and it degrades to **O(n²)**. The recursion uses **O(log n)** stack on average, O(n) in that worst case.

blocks.alt: Best and average: O(n log n) time, O(log n) space. Worst: bad pivots: O(n²) time, O(n) space.

blocks.text: The usual fix is a **random pivot**: swap a random value of the range into `nums[hi]` before partitioning. Then no particular input is reliably bad, and O(n²) becomes vanishingly unlikely. Production versions also pick the median of three values and switch to insertion sort for tiny ranges.

items: **Not stable** — partition swaps can jump a value over an equal one.
**In-place** — only the recursion stack is extra.
**Very fast in practice** — tight loops over contiguous memory make it the fastest comparison sort on random arrays.

blocks.text: It's the general-purpose in-memory sort: C++'s `std::sort` is introsort (quick sort that switches to heap sort if the recursion goes too deep), and Java sorts primitives with dual-pivot quick sort. Its partition step is a pattern on its own — Sort Colors, Sort Array By Parity and Kth Largest Element (quickselect) are all partitions.

items: **Partition** around a pivot so it lands in its final place, then sort both sides.
**O(n log n)** on average, **O(n²)** with consistently bad pivots — randomise the pivot.
**In-place** but **not stable**; usually the fastest sort for arrays in memory.
